title: Indian Diaspora in North Texas Celebrates 80th Independence Day With Grand Cultural Fest
excerpt: IANT's 49th Anand Bazaar drew thousands to Comerica Center in Frisco, combining India's Independence Day and America's 250th anniversary celebrations.
body:
• The India Association of North Texas hosted its 49th Anand Bazaar at Comerica Center in Frisco on August 15, celebrating both India's 80th Independence Day and America's 250th anniversary
  • The free event featured cultural performances, an Independence Day parade, vendor booths, a children's play area, and a musical concert
  • Multiple celebrations across the DFW area — including a flag hoisting at Mahatma Gandhi Memorial Plaza in Plano — underscored the vibrancy of North Texas's Indian community

The India Association of North Texas (IANT) hosted its 49th annual Anand Bazaar at Comerica Center in Frisco on Saturday, August 15, bringing together thousands of Indian Americans in the Dallas-Fort Worth area to celebrate India's 80th Independence Day. The event also marked America's 250th anniversary, weaving together patriotic themes from both nations in one of the region's largest community gatherings.

Admission was free, with the celebration kicking off at 2:00 PM and running through the evening with a packed schedule of cultural programming.

A Full Day of Festivities

The event featured an Independence Day parade through the venue, live cultural performances showcasing Indian classical, folk, and Bollywood dance, vendor booths offering Indian apparel, jewelry, food, and community services, and a dedicated children's play area. The day culminated in a musical concert that drew enthusiastic crowds.

Dignitary speeches and community recognition segments honored individuals and organizations contributing to the Indian-American community in North Texas. IANT, one of the oldest Indian community organizations in the DFW metroplex, has hosted Anand Bazaar annually for nearly five decades, making it a cornerstone event for the diaspora.

This year's move to Comerica Center — the 4,500-seat indoor arena that serves as home to the Texas Legends basketball team — represented an upgrade from previous years when the event was held at Frisco RoughRiders Stadium, reflecting the growing scale and ambition of the celebration.

Celebrations Across the Metroplex

Anand Bazaar was not the only Independence Day event in North Texas. At the Mahatma Gandhi Memorial Plaza (MGMNT) in Plano, a flag hoisting ceremony began at 8:00 AM on August 15, with breakfast served to attendees. The MGMNT events have become a morning tradition for the community, with families gathering for the tricolor ceremony before attending afternoon festivities elsewhere.

The Hindu Temple of Greater Fort Worth hosted its own cultural evening at 7:00 PM, and the week saw additional events including a meet-and-greet with legendary Indian film composer Ilaiyaraaja at Bharat Bhavan in Irving on August 14 — drawing music enthusiasts from across the metroplex.

A Growing Community's Annual Tradition

IANT's 2026 event calendar reflects the breadth of North Texas's Indian-American community, spanning Republic Day celebrations, International Yoga Day, volleyball tournaments, a Gandhi Peace Walk, and Thanksgiving lunches served to local police departments and first responders. The organization has long positioned itself as a bridge between the Indian community and broader civic life in the DFW area.

The dual celebration of Indian and American independence days has become particularly resonant for diaspora families navigating life between two cultures. With America marking its 250th anniversary this year, several Indian-American organizations across the country used August 15 as an occasion to honor their connection to both nations.

Part of a Nationwide Wave

The North Texas celebrations were part of a broader wave of Indian Independence Day events across the United States. In Houston, the Consul General of India, D.C. Manjunath, attended festivities and hoisted the tricolor at India House. In the Bay Area, the Festival of Globe organized a week-long celebration. Events were also held in Atlanta, Nashville, Indianapolis, Fort Lauderdale, and other cities with large Indian-American populations — each marking 80 years of Indian independence with cultural performances, food, and community gatherings.
